passage: On the first Monday of term, the teacher at the village school did not read out rules. She gave each child a slip of paper. “Write one thing that would help us learn together,” she said. Arohi, who had been laughed at before for reading slowly, wrote “No mocking” with a shaking pencil. Mehak wrote “Listen when others talk.” A boy called Sunil wrote “No rules,” and the class giggled. The teacher read them all out, and the children voted on the list with raised hands. Sunil grudgingly raised his. The chart went up beside the blackboard with every child's thumbprint. A week later Mehak told a boy who was talking over Arohi, “That's our rule.”

qa.q: What did Arohi write on her slip of paper?
qa.a: Arohi wrote “No mocking” on her slip.

qa.q: Why did Arohi's pencil shake when she wrote “No mocking”?
qa.a: Arohi was probably nervous, having been laughed at before for reading slowly, so writing “No mocking” took courage and mattered a lot to her.

qa.q: Why might the rules on the chart be followed more willingly than rules read out by the teacher?
qa.a: The children wrote and voted on them and pressed their thumbprints on the chart, so the rules feel like theirs and not something imposed.

qa.q: What might Sunil be thinking when he grudgingly raises his hand for the list?
qa.a: Sunil may still be unsure about rules but does not want to be the only one left out, so he goes along; being part of the vote may make the chart feel a little his too.

grounding: A teacher and class create shared rules together, such as listening and no mocking, and the children follow them because they helped make them.

passage: In Mrs Greene's classroom, the second Friday of the school year was spent building a class charter. Yosef held the marker. The children shouted ideas: “Listen to each other,” “Raise a hand,” “No making fun.” Ivan called out “No homework on Fridays,” and everybody laughed, including the teacher. “Let's try to keep it about how we treat each other,” she said. Ivan shrugged, then suggested “Say sorry when you mess up,” and the class cheered. Everyone signed the poster. The following week, when Ivan interrupted a quiet girl, Yosef pointed at the poster without a word. Ivan went pink, sat back and said, “Sorry. Go on.”

qa.q: Who held the marker while the class built the charter?
qa.a: Yosef held the marker.

qa.q: Why might Ivan have suggested “Say sorry when you mess up”?
qa.a: Ivan probably wanted to help make a rule the class would really use after the joke about Friday homework was set aside, which shows Ivan took part in the making.

qa.q: What made the poster work when Ivan interrupted a quiet girl?
qa.a: The class had made and signed the poster together, so a silent point from Yosef was enough to remind Ivan of a rule Ivan had helped write.

qa.q: What might the quiet girl have felt when Ivan said, “Sorry. Go on”?
qa.a: The girl probably felt relieved and heard, since the interruption stopped and she was invited to continue. 🙂

grounding: A teacher and class write shared agreements, and children follow rules they helped make more willingly than imposed ones.

passage: At the community centre's Saturday art club, paint water kept getting spilled on other people's work, and the arguments were getting louder. Nandini, the volunteer teacher, didn't announce a rule. She put a big sheet of chart paper on the floor. 'What would make this room fair for everyone?' Zeenat said, 'No touching someone's painting without asking.' A boy added, 'No laughing at bad drawings.' Someone else said, 'Only one water jar per table.' They argued, voted and wrote seven rules in fat markers. Everyone signed at the bottom, even the youngest, who drew a star. The next Saturday, when Pintu reached for Zeenat's brush, three children pointed at the chart before Nandini could speak. Pintu pulled his hand back and asked first.

qa.q: How many rules did the art club write?
qa.a: Seven rules, in fat markers.

qa.q: How might Zeenat have felt when the others pointed at the chart?
qa.a: Zeenat likely felt protected and proud, since the rule Zeenat suggested was now defended by the whole group.

qa.q: Why did the chart work better than Nandini simply announcing rules?
qa.a: The children suggested, argued, voted and signed the rules themselves, so they felt the rules were theirs and upheld them.

qa.q: What is it like for Pintu when three children point at the chart?
qa.a: He is checked by his peers, not scolded by an adult, so he likely feels a little embarrassed but simply asks instead.

grounding: A teacher and children make shared rules together, and the children then keep them willingly.

passage: My name is Lavanya, and I sit near the door in Class 5A, so I see everything. After the bad week, when two boys fought over the cricket bat and the whole class was shouting, Mr Kamal didn't punish anyone. On Monday he asked us to make our own class promises. At first nobody spoke. Then Gayatri said, 'Listen when someone is talking.' Arun said, 'No names that hurt.' Mr Kamal wrote each one down and asked, 'Can everyone keep this?' We changed 'never shout' to 'use a normal voice', because Arun said nobody could never shout. By Friday, I noticed something. When Rinku started teasing, it wasn't sir who stopped him, it was Arun. 'Promise number two,' Arun said. I don't know if Arun really changed inside, but he seemed to like being the one who remembered.

qa.q: Why did the class change 'never shout'?
qa.a: Because Arun said nobody could never shout, so it became 'use a normal voice'.

qa.q: What does Arun saying 'Promise number two' suggest about him?
qa.a: He seems proud and invested in the rules, liking being the one who remembers a promise he helped write.

qa.q: What did Mr Kamal do instead of punishing anyone, and why did it work?
qa.a: He asked the class to make its own promises and checked that everyone could keep them, so the children followed and upheld the rules willingly.

qa.q: How might Rinku feel being stopped by a classmate rather than the teacher?
qa.a: He may feel a bit embarrassed, but hearing it from a peer shows the rule belongs to the whole class, not just to the teacher.

grounding: A classmate's account of a class and teacher making their own promises, which the children then keep more willingly.

passage: June: Harish sir pinned a printed list of ten rules above the board. By the second day, Vikas and his friends were making paper planes out of the spare copy. July, a rainy Monday: sir took the list down. 'It isn't working. Let's write our own.' Vikas, half joking, suggested 'No homework on Fridays.' Sir laughed and wrote it under 'maybe'. The class argued for forty minutes, then settled on five rules, including 'Nobody laughs when someone reads slowly.' Vikas proposed that one, thinking of his cousin Manu, who sat two rows behind and stammered. August: when a new boy stumbled over a word, Vikas turned around and gave the gigglers a look. Nobody made paper planes out of the new list. It had all their signatures on it.

qa.q: How many rules did the class settle on?
qa.a: Five rules.

qa.q: Why did Vikas propose the rule about slow readers?
qa.a: He was thinking of his cousin Manu, who stammered, and felt protective of anyone who reads slowly.

qa.q: What made the class keep the new list when they had ignored the first one?
qa.a: They argued, chose and signed the rules themselves, so the list felt like theirs, not something pinned up for them.

qa.q: What is it like for the new boy when Vikas gives the gigglers a look?
qa.a: He is likely relieved and less embarrassed, because a classmate stops the laughing before it grows.

grounding: Over three months a class moves from ignoring imposed rules to keeping rules they made together with their teacher.

passage: Sit, Nirmala, I'll tell you about my Class 5, back in Madurai. I'm your Yamini Paati now, but then I was a skinny girl of nine with two plaits. Our new teacher, Mr Joseph, didn't write rules on the board. He asked us, "What makes a class good to be in?" Selvi said, "Nobody laughs when you're wrong." Raghu said, "Let people finish talking." We argued about "no shouting" for ten whole minutes! Then all thirty-two of us signed the chart in our own handwriting. Funny thing: when Raghu himself interrupted one day, it was tiny Selvi who pointed at the chart, and he stopped. Nobody ever obeyed the old teacher's rules like that. These were ours, you see.

qa.q: How many children signed the chart?
qa.a: All thirty-two of them signed the chart in their own handwriting.

qa.q: How can you tell young Yamini felt proud of the class rules?
qa.a: She still remembers the ten-minute argument and says the rules "were ours", which shows pride and a sense of ownership.

qa.q: Which choice of Mr Joseph's was the turning point, and why?
qa.a: He asked the class what makes a good class instead of writing rules himself, so the children owned the rules and followed them willingly.

qa.q: Why might Raghu have stopped when Selvi pointed at the chart?
qa.a: Raghu had helped make the rule about letting people finish, so a reminder from a classmate felt fair rather than like a telling-off from above.

grounding: Yamini Paati remembers a teacher and class making shared rules, which the children then followed more willingly than imposed ones.
